section.title: The Sins of Jerusalem
section.sectionRationale: This chapter presents Jerusalem as 'the city of bloodshed,' cataloguing an almost exhaustive list of sins, violence by princes, oppression of the vulnerable, sexual abominations, bribery, and forgetting God entirely, before turning to two vivid images of coming judgment: Israel as dross to be melted in a smelting furnace, and the sobering statement that God searched for just one person to stand in the gap and found no one.
section.thesis: Jerusalem's corruption runs through every level of society, princes, priests, officials, prophets, and people alike, so completely that God's own search for a single faithful intercessor to stand in the gap comes up empty, exposing humanity's total inability to supply its own mediator and driving the reader to Christ, the one true Mediator who stands in the gap perfectly where every human candidate failed.
section.frameNote: Five movements: Jerusalem, a city of bloodshed, brings her own doom; a catalogue of her sins, violence, oppression, and forgetting God; judgment announced as scattering among the nations to purge uncleanness; Israel pictured as dross to be melted in a smelting furnace; and a final survey of corruption in every class, closing with God's search for someone to stand in the gap, and finding no one.

units.label: A city of bloodshed brings her own doom
units.note: guilt from bloodshed and idolatry alike

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“As for you, son of man, will you judge her? Will you pass judgment on the city of bloodshed? Then confront her with all her abominations
and tell her that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘O city who brings her own doom by shedding {{dam|blood}} within her walls and making idols to defile herself,

you are guilty of the blood you have shed, and you are defiled by the idols you have made. You have brought your days to a close and have come to the end of your years. Therefore I have made you a reproach to the nations and a mockery to all the lands.
Those near and far will mock you, O infamous city, full of turmoil.

units.label: A catalogue of Jerusalem's sins
units.note: violence, idolatry, oppression, and forgetting God

verses.text: See how every prince of Israel within you has used his power to shed blood.
Father and mother are treated with contempt. Within your walls the foreign resident is exploited, the fatherless and the widow are oppressed.
You have despised My holy things and {{chalal|profaned}} My Sabbaths.
Among you are slanderous men bent on bloodshed; within you are those who eat on the mountain shrines and commit acts of indecency.
In you they have uncovered the nakedness of their fathers; in you they violate women during their menstrual impurity.
One man commits an abomination with his neighbor's wife; another wickedly defiles his daughter-in-law; and yet another violates his sister, his own father's daughter.
In you they take bribes to shed blood. You engage in usury, take excess interest, and extort your neighbors. But Me you have forgotten, declares the Lord GOD.
Now look, I strike My hands together against your unjust gain and against the blood you have shed in your midst.
Will your courage endure or your hands be strong in the day I deal with you? I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will act.
I will disperse you among the nations and scatter you throughout the lands; I will purge your uncleanness.
And when you have defiled yourself in the eyes of the nations, then you will know that I am the LORD.’”

units.label: Israel becomes dross in the furnace

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, the house of Israel has become {{sig|dross}} to Me. All of them are copper, tin, iron, and lead inside the furnace; they are but the dross of silver.
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Because all of you have become dross, behold, I will gather you into Jerusalem.
Just as one gathers silver, copper, iron, lead, and tin into the furnace to melt with a fiery blast, so I will gather you in My anger and wrath, leave you there, and melt you.
Yes, I will gather you together and blow on you with the fire of My wrath, and you will be melted within the city.
As silver is melted in a furnace, so you will be melted within the city. Then you will know that I, the LORD, have poured out My wrath upon you.’”

units.label: Every class corrupt; no one to stand in the gap
units.note: princes, priests, officials, prophets, and people alike

verses.text: And the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, say to her, ‘In the day of indignation, you are a land that has not been cleansed, upon which no rain has fallen.’
The conspiracy of the princes in her midst is like a roaring lion tearing its prey. They devour the people, seize the treasures and precious things, and multiply the widows within her.

Her priests do violence to My law and profane My holy things. They make no distinction between the holy and the common, and they fail to distinguish between the clean and the unclean. They disregard My Sabbaths, so that I am profaned among them.
Her officials within her are like wolves tearing their prey, shedding blood, and destroying lives for dishonest gain.
Her prophets whitewash these deeds by false visions and lying divinations, saying, ‘This is what the Lord GOD says,’ when the LORD has not spoken.
The people of the land have practiced extortion and committed robbery. They have oppressed the poor and needy and have exploited the foreign resident without justice.
I searched for a man among them to repair the wall and stand in the {{perets|gap}} before Me on behalf of the land, so that I should not destroy it. But I found no one.
So I have poured out My indignation upon them and consumed them with the fire of My fury. I have brought their ways down upon their own heads, declares the Lord GOD.”

dam.gloss: Blood, specifically shed blood, bloodguilt. Jerusalem is repeatedly named 'the city of bloodshed,' verses 2-3, her violence against the vulnerable, treated by princes, officials, and citizens alike as the central charge running through this whole indictment.

chalal.gloss: To profane, defile, or treat as common what is holy. Applied here to the Sabbath, and later to the priests themselves, verse 26, who fail to distinguish holy from common, showing how thoroughly Jerusalem's corruption had erased the very distinctions meant to mark her out as God's people.

sig.gloss: Dross, the impure waste skimmed off in metal refining. Applied to the whole house of Israel, this image reframes the coming exile not merely as punishment but as a smelting process, though here, unusually, no pure metal is promised to remain, only judgment poured out.

perets.gloss: A breach or gap in a wall, used metaphorically of a moral and intercessory breach needing someone to stand in it, deflecting judgment. God searched for such an intercessor and 'found no one,' a stark verdict that anticipates the true Intercessor, Christ, who stands in the gap once for all.

basic.context: This chapter presents Jerusalem as 'the city of bloodshed,' cataloguing an almost exhaustive list of sins, violence by princes, oppression of the vulnerable, sexual abominations, bribery, and forgetting God entirely, before turning to two vivid images of coming judgment: Israel as dross to be melted in a smelting furnace, and the sobering statement that God searched for just one person to stand in the gap and found no one.
basic.hermeneutics: This is an extended prophetic indictment, moving through three linked oracles: a general charge of bloodshed and idolatry, a smelting-furnace image of coming judgment as refinement, and a final class-by-class survey of corruption, princes, priests, officials, prophets, and people, that leaves no one exempt and no intercessor found.
basic.originalLanguages: Jerusalem is 'the city of dam, bloodshed,' whose holy things are chalal, profaned, by prince and priest alike. God pictures the nation as sig, dross, to be melted in judgment's furnace, and closes by searching for someone to stand in the perets, breach or gap, in the wall, an intercessor who might turn back His wrath. He finds no one.
basic.typology: God's search for someone to 'stand in the gap' and finding none anticipates the one perfect Intercessor who does stand in the gap for sinners once and for all, Jesus Christ, who both bears the judgment this chapter describes and intercedes without failure where every human mediator fell short.
basic.christ: Verse 30's devastating search, 'I searched for a man among them to repair the wall and stand in the gap... but I found no one,' exposes humanity's complete inability to provide its own mediator. The New Testament answers this exact need in Christ, the one Mediator between God and man, 1 Timothy 2:5, who stands in the gap fully, both absorbing the judgment this chapter describes and interceding perfectly for His people, Hebrews 7:25.
basic.god: God is the offended holy judge, personally cataloguing Jerusalem's sins against the vulnerable, against His own holy things, and against Himself, 'Me you have forgotten'; yet He is also the one actively searching for a rescuer to spare the city, showing that judgment here is not eager but reluctant, sought against only after every possibility of mercy through human intercession has been exhausted.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 1:21-26 similarly pictures Jerusalem's dross needing to be refined by judgment. Ezekiel 13:5 already faults false prophets for failing to 'stand in the gap' before this final indictment. 1 Timothy 2:5 names Christ as the one Mediator between God and man. Hebrews 7:25 describes Christ as always living to intercede for His people, the perfect answer to verse 30's failed search.
basic.oneStory: This is the moment God's search for a single faithful intercessor in Jerusalem comes up completely empty, exposing the total moral collapse of every class of leadership and the desperate need for a mediator no sinner could supply. That need finds its full and final answer in Jesus Christ, the one who stands in the gap perfectly, absorbing judgment and interceding without fail for all who trust Him.

context.literary:
The chapter is three oracles, each opened by the same formula, 'the word of the LORD came to me,' at verses 1, 17 and 23, and each ends on a verdict that begins to sound final: the days are closed, verse 4, the city will be melted, verse 22, and the fire of fury has been poured out, verse 31. The first oracle (verses 1 to 16) is a prosecution. The second (verses 17 to 22) is a metalworker's parable. The third (verses 23 to 31) is a survey of leadership class by class, ending with the line that does the most work in the whole chapter, the search for someone in the breach and the sentence, 'But I found no one.'

The opening is courtroom language. The prophet is asked, 'will you judge her?' in verse 2, which makes him an advocate whom the Lord invites to examine the evidence before the sentence is read. The charge sheet that follows is arranged by relationship: shed blood, idols and the Sabbath, then the family and the neighbour, then money, and the whole list ends with a single hinge sentence, 'But Me you have forgotten,' verse 12. Everything before is a symptom and that clause is the disease.

The two images that follow share a rare feature: they appear to promise cleansing and then deny it. A furnace usually leaves silver behind, but verse 18 lists copper, tin, iron and lead and no silver at all. A land should be washed by rain, but verse 24 says there is none. The third oracle works through the stations of Jerusalem's society as a flowing list, princes, priests, officials, prophets and people, each with its own animal or metaphor, lion, wolf, whitewash, and the verdict ends on the unfilled gap.
context.historical:
The chapter is undated, but it sits between the oracles of 591 BC at 20:1 and the beginning of the siege at 24:1, so it belongs to the last years of Judah. As the war drew near, people fell back on the fortified cities, compare Jeremiah 4:5 and 8:14, so the capital would have been crowded, which gives verse 19, 'I will gather you into Jerusalem,' a grim literal edge. The city that was meant to be a refuge became a smelter.

The sin list reads like a walk through the Holiness Code of Leviticus. Contempt for parents, verse 7, recalls Leviticus 19:3 and 20:9. The abuse of the foreign resident, the widow and the fatherless, verse 7, touches Exodus 22:21 to 22 and Leviticus 19:33. Slander that endangers life, verse 9, is Leviticus 19:16. The sexual crimes of verses 10 and 11 follow the order and the vocabulary of Leviticus 18. Usury, verse 12, is forbidden among kinsmen in Leviticus 25:36, and bribes to shed blood violate Exodus 23:8. The first hearers would have recognised every item. This was not a new moral code applied unfairly. It was the covenant they had heard read.

The priests' failure in verse 26 is exact: they do not distinguish 'between the holy and the common,' which is the very task given to Aaron's house in Leviticus 10:10. The prophets 'whitewash,' verse 28, as Ezekiel 13:10 to 15 had charged, and Jeremiah 6:14 and 8:11 say of the prophets and priests of the same generation that they treat the people's wound lightly. The picture of wolves and lions has a long pedigree. Zephaniah, a generation earlier, had called Jerusalem's princes roaring lions and her judges evening wolves, Zephaniah 3:3, and her prophets and priests the same, verse 4.
context.canonical:
The smelting image has a long career in the prophets. Isaiah 1:22 and 25 speaks of silver turned to dross and of a purging that removes the dross and impurities, where the end of the fire is purity. Jeremiah 6:28 to 30 looks at the same process and finds it fails: the bellows blow, the lead is not drawn off, and the people are called rejected silver. Ezekiel stands closer to Jeremiah than to Isaiah. In his version the metals go in and nothing precious comes out. Later prophets pick the image up again with a better ending, Zechariah 13:9 and Malachi 3:2 to 3, where God sits as a refiner and purifier of silver and the sons of Levi are refined.

The search for a person 'to repair the wall and stand in the gap' belongs with a whole family of intercession texts. Abraham bargains for Sodom down to ten, Genesis 18:32. Moses stands 'in the breach' to turn aside wrath, Psalm 106:23, and offers to be blotted out, Exodus 32:32. Jeremiah is told the Lord would not hear even Moses and Samuel, Jeremiah 15:1. Isaiah says of the Lord, 'He saw that there was no man; He was amazed that there was no one to intercede, so His own arm brought salvation,' Isaiah 59:16, and again at Isaiah 63:5.

The New Testament takes up that last note. Jesus is the one mediator, 1 Timothy 2:5, who always lives to intercede, Hebrews 7:25, and who is called our advocate, 1 John 2:1. Revelation 5:2 to 5 repeats Ezekiel's structure in the heavenly court, where no one is found worthy until the Lion of Judah appears.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel wanted his hearers to stop treating Jerusalem's fall as an accident of politics. The chapter takes away every alibi in turn. The exiles could not say it was the princes alone, because the people of the land are indicted in verse 29. They could not say it was the other class, the priests or the prophets, since each class is named. And they could not say the Lord had never warned them, since the charges are the commands they had been given.

The unusual pattern of the sin list, with household sins sitting beside political and cultic ones, was meant to teach that holiness is one fabric. A city that has stopped honouring parents and sheltering the stranger is the same city that profanes the Sabbath and bribes the judge. Idolatry was not a private matter separate from justice. The root, verse 12, is forgetting God.

The last verse sets a trap for the self-excusing. Ezekiel's hearers might say that someone should have stood in the gap, and the text says that someone was sought. That leaves each reader with the uncomfortable question of whether he is part of the unremarkable crowd or a person who would have gone up to the breach. It also prepares the exiles for a hard truth: the only hope will not come from within the people's own supply.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes judgment on one city whose sins were specific, and it gives a diagnosis rather than a method. Reading it as a template for how God will treat any modern city is risky. The New Testament does not say that nations stand where Jerusalem stood, but it does apply the principle to the church, 1 Peter 4:17, where judgment begins with the household of God.

The sins listed are not endorsed; the laws they break are the standard. Much of the list reaffirms commands that remain in force in the New Testament, such as honouring parents and caring for the vulnerable, while the ritual categories of Leviticus 18 and 19 apply differently to those who are in Christ, Acts 15 and Colossians 2:16 to 17.

The search for an intercessor is not a command to pray in a general sense but a statement of what God was looking for. Yet it still instructs. Believers are told to make intercessions for all, 1 Timothy 2:1, and the question 'would I stand in the gap?' is a fair one. The safe way to ask it is to remember that the only one who fully stands there is Christ, and our intercession is a share in His, not an attempt to replace it.

debates.question: Was Jerusalem's rescue ever really possible, verse 30?

views.label: A real offer that went unmet
views.case: God had said to Jeremiah that one person who acts justly would have led Him to forgive the city, Jeremiah 5:1, and Abraham's bargaining for Sodom assumes that the number of the righteous mattered, Genesis 18:32. On this reading the search is sincere and the empty result is the tragedy.

views.label: A statement of the people's depth of guilt, not an open door
views.case: Ezekiel 14:14 says that even Noah, Daniel and Job would save only themselves, and Jeremiah 15:1 says even Moses and Samuel would not turn God's heart. Judgment was already set, and the search shows how complete the corruption was rather than how close the rescue came.

views.label: Both: the offer is real, but the guilt is sufficient
views.case: The text can carry both. God does search, and the invitation is genuine, but He knew what He would find, much as He asked Adam where he was. The question is for the sake of the hearers, so that they cannot say no one asked.

debates.bearing: The passage is best read as an indictment, not a cosmic puzzle. It does not say a single intercessor could have undone a century of sin, nor does it say intercession is pointless. It says that the people who ought to have gone up to the wall, 13:5, did not, and that the failure was theirs.

debates.question: Is the furnace an act of punishment or purification?

views.label: Punishment, with no refining result
views.case: Verse 18 lists only base metals, and verse 22 ends with 'you will know that I, the LORD, have poured out My wrath.' Jeremiah 6:29 to 30 says the refining proceeds in vain. The point is that there is nothing of value to extract.

views.label: Purification in the long run
views.case: Verse 15 says, 'I will purge your uncleanness,' and the same book moves from judgment to cleansing, 36:25 to 27. Isaiah 1:25 and Malachi 3:3 use the furnace for real refining.

views.label: Judgment that makes purification possible
views.case: Some say the furnace in this chapter is the destructive stage, and the later chapters are the new work. The fire does not itself make them clean, but it removes the false security that would keep them from the new heart.

debates.bearing: All three can be true at different levels. The immediate text is punishment and says so, but the book as a whole does not leave the people in the fire. What changes in Ezekiel is not the metal but the gift of a new spirit, and the fire clears the ground for it.

study.originalLanguages:
The first charge in the chapter is that the city is 'the city of bloodshed,' literally a city of bloods. The plural dam is the Hebrew idiom for blood that has been shed, bloodguilt, and it is a favourite of Ezekiel's, appearing in 22:2, 24:6 and 24:9. The verb in verse 3 for the city 'shedding' that blood is shaphak, the verb used elsewhere for pouring out, and God uses the same verb when He pours out His wrath at verses 22 and 31. The punishment is shaped like the crime: they poured out blood, and He pours out fury.

The sentence in verse 4 that the city has 'brought her days to a close' uses a verb meaning to draw near. The close of her days is something she herself has summoned. The next word is the name she will carry among the nations, a reproach and a mockery, and verse 5 adds that she is 'infamous' and 'full of turmoil,' labels that attach to the city rather than to any one act.

The word the BSB translates 'indecency,' zimmah, in verse 9, covers planned wickedness and sexual crime alike. Ezekiel 22:9 to 11 uses it for the long list of family sins, and the same word returns in Ezekiel 16 and 23. The usury of verse 12 uses two terms, neshek and tarbit, the two words Leviticus 25:36 puts together when it forbids charging a brother 'interest or profit.' Ezekiel is not offering a new category but citing the law as it stands.

The central image, 'dross,' sig, is the scum thrown off when metal melts. Verse 18 says the house of Israel has become dross to Me, and the whole nation is that scum. The 'furnace' of the passage, kur, is the word used for Egypt as an 'iron furnace' in Deuteronomy 4:20. The people God brought out of the furnace are now put into one again. There is bitter irony in the reversal.

The word at the heart of verse 30, perets, 'breach' or 'gap,' means a breaking-through, as in a wall that has been breached. Psalm 106:23 uses the very expression of Moses standing 'in the breach.' The verb for 'repair,' gadar, means to wall up or build a barrier and is from the family of words for a wall or fence. The two together describe not a general prayer but a specific act: getting between the attacker and the opening.

In verse 28 the prophets say, 'This is what the Lord GOD says,' when the LORD has not spoken. The abuse is of the messenger formula itself. The formula is real, and the claim that goes with it is false, which is why the chapter treats it as an attack on God's own name.

typology.fulfillment: Moses stood 'in the breach' to turn aside wrath, offering even to be blotted out of God's book, Exodus 32:32. He is the great pattern of the man Ezekiel 22:30 was looking for. Jesus is the greater Moses: the Mediator who does not merely offer His life but gives it, 1 Timothy 2:5 to 6, and who 'bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors,' Isaiah 53:12. The pattern falls short because Moses interceded as a sinner among sinners and could not be a full substitute, while Christ intercedes as one who has no sin of His own, Hebrews 7:26 to 27.

Israel was brought out of Egypt's iron furnace and in this chapter is put into a furnace again. The same image carries into Malachi 3:2 to 3, where the Lord sits as a refiner of silver, and into 1 Peter 1:7, where faith is tested as gold is tried by fire. In Christ the fire is borne by Him first: He passes through the heat of God's wrath on the cross, so that those who trust Him go through trial and are refined, not consumed. The correspondence is a theme and not a one-to-one allegory, and it breaks where Ezekiel's furnace yields no silver at all.

typology.type: The wall that no one repaired
typology.fulfillment: The Lord looks for someone to 'repair the wall.' Nehemiah later rebuilds the physical wall after the exile, Nehemiah 2:17, a partial answer and a sign of the grace that follows judgment. The true wall repair is Christ, who 'is our peace' and has broken down the dividing wall of hostility, Ephesians 2:14. The type is imperfect because Nehemiah's wall had to be rebuilt again and again, while Christ's work is done once for all, Hebrews 10:12.

Jerusalem is called a land not cleansed and not rained on, verse 24, a picture of dryness under judgment. The prophet's later hope is of clean water sprinkled, Ezekiel 36:25. Jesus cries out in the Temple that rivers of living water will flow from the one who believes in Him, John 7:37 to 39, which John says refers to the Spirit. The link is by contrast and promise, drawn from the book's own movement, and it falls short only in that Ezekiel's text does not itself yet name the Giver.

study.christ:
The chapter's closing sentence is a vacancy notice. God looked for a man to repair the wall and stand in the gap and found no one. That absence is the shape into which the New Testament pours the person of Jesus, and the case for it rests on the way the Bible itself keeps returning to the search.

Isaiah makes the connection nearly explicit. 'He saw that there was no man; He was amazed that there was no one to intercede, so His own arm brought salvation,' Isaiah 59:16. In Ezekiel the vacancy ends in fire; in Isaiah the vacancy is filled by God's own arm. The Gospels present Jesus as that arm. He is the 'one mediator between God and men,' 1 Timothy 2:5, the one who 'always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:25, and the advocate with the Father, 1 John 2:1. Where Moses stood in the breach and could only offer his own life, Exodus 32:32, Jesus gives His, and Isaiah 53:12 says He 'made intercession for the transgressors.'

The depth of the corruption matters for how we hear this. The chapter reaches every class: princes, priests, officials, prophets and the people of the land. No one is left from whom a mediator might come. It is the same logic as Paul's, 'all have sinned,' Romans 3:23, applied here to a city. The mediator has to come from outside the human supply, and yet be human, which is exactly what 1 Timothy 2:5 says: 'the man Christ Jesus.'

Revelation 5 repeats the scene. In the heavenly court a scroll of judgment is held out and the angel asks who is worthy. 'No one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able,' verse 3, and John weeps. Then he is told, 'Do not weep! Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed,' verse 5. The structure is the same as Ezekiel 22:30, a search and an empty result, except that this time a candidate is found.

The leaders of the chapter are shepherd-failures: lions and wolves who devour the flock. Jesus identifies Himself as the good shepherd who lays down His life, in contrast to the hired hand who runs when he sees the wolf, John 10:11 to 12. Ezekiel 34, soon after, promises that the Lord Himself will shepherd the sheep, and Jesus claims that role.

Finally, the furnace and the wrath are not escaped but borne. The chapter says God will pour out His fury on Jerusalem, verse 31, and the New Testament says that the Son bore the cost of that wrath as the propitiation for our sins, Romans 3:25 and 1 John 2:2. Those who believe do not stand in a furnace where nothing precious remains, since 'there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus,' Romans 8:1.

Care is needed. The verse does not mention a coming Messiah, and the reading depends on the pattern of intercession across Scripture and the New Testament's use of it. It would be a mistake to say Ezekiel foresaw Jesus in verse 30. The better claim is that the text exposes a need only He fills.
study.god:
This chapter gives a portrait of a God who takes account. He knows the exact crimes and names them, from the bribe taken in a courtroom to the abuse done in a household. The detail is not for the sake of drama; it shows that nothing in Jerusalem was hidden from Him. The God who says 'But Me you have forgotten,' verse 12, is not the distant clockmaker whom the people had come to imagine. He is personally wounded by the forgetting, and He keeps the books.

He is also holy in a way that touches ordinary life. His 'holy things' and His Sabbaths, verse 8, are despised in the same breath as the neglect of widows. The chapter will not let anyone separate worship from justice. A God who cares about the ledger of a loan, verse 12, is a God whose holiness has an address in the neighbourhood.

He is a God who judges according to the sin's own shape. The city poured out blood and He pours out wrath, verses 3, 22 and 31. The people gathered themselves into Jerusalem and He gathers them into the furnace, verse 19. This is a measured justice, not a random one, and it shows that the sentence is the result of what they chose.

He is a God who searches. The search for a person in the gap is among the most arresting sentences about God in the Old Testament. Not because God lacks knowledge, but because it reveals what He wants: He would rather forgive than destroy, 'so that I should not destroy it,' verse 30. It shows that judgment is the last option and that He keeps looking until He finds none. Compare Ezekiel 18:23, where He asks whether He takes any pleasure in the death of the wicked.

At the same time God stays free. He was not obliged to let the search succeed, and the dross is melted. The text keeps both truths in view: He desires mercy and yet will not pretend that a city of bloodshed is clean.

For worship, the chapter teaches that the right response to God's holiness is neither indifference nor panic but repentance together with honest confession that we are no better than the city, followed by gratitude that He has provided the one the city could not.

crossReferences.note: The catalogue of forbidden sexual relationships in Leviticus 18 lines up closely with the crimes of Ezekiel 22:10 to 11, including the nakedness of a father, a neighbour's wife, a daughter-in-law and a sister. Ezekiel is reading the covenant law back to a people who had stopped keeping it.

The priests are to distinguish between the holy and the common and between the clean and the unclean. Ezekiel 22:26 charges that they made no such distinction. The verse shows that the priests' failure was not subtle: they abandoned the one task that defined their office.

A generation earlier Zephaniah described Jerusalem's princes as roaring lions, her judges as wolves, her prophets as reckless and her priests as doing violence to the law. The agreement with Ezekiel 22:25 to 28 shows that the corruption was not a late event but an inherited pattern across classes.

Jeremiah's image of refining silver ends with the bellows blasting and the lead not drawn off, so that the people are called rejected silver. It is the nearest parallel to Ezekiel's furnace and shows that both prophets saw the fire as failing to purify, not because the fire was weak but because there was no silver to be had.

Isaiah says Jerusalem's silver has become dross and that God will purge the dross and remove all impurities. Where Ezekiel sees only dross, Isaiah's furnace leaves something. Together they give the two sides of the fire, wrath that melts and mercy that cleanses.

Earlier in the book the false prophets are charged with not going up to the gaps or restoring the wall so that it might stand in the battle on the day of the LORD. Chapter 22 returns to the same picture and widens the charge to all, so that verse 30 reads as the climax of a theme.

The Lord says that even Noah, Daniel and Job, were they in the land, would save only themselves by their righteousness. It stands as a sober counterweight to the search of 22:30, reminding readers that judgment on Judah did not hang on a missing intercessor alone.

Moses goes up to the Lord to seek atonement for the golden calf and asks that, if forgiveness is not given, he himself be blotted out of God's book. His readiness to stand in for the people is the standard against which the empty search in Ezekiel is measured.

The Lord saw that there was no man and was amazed that there was no one to intercede, so His own arm brought salvation. It states the same situation as Ezekiel 22:30 and adds the answer: when no human intercessor is found, God Himself provides one.

Paul pairs one God with a single go-between and names him as a human being, Christ Jesus. The line says the empty gap of Ezekiel 22 is filled by someone who is truly one of us, and it explains why the Old Testament's repeated search kept ending in disappointment.

Jesus is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them. The tense of a continual intercession answers a city where no one stood even once.

A search is made in heaven and on earth for one who is worthy to open the scroll, and no one is found until the Lion of the tribe of Judah appears. The pattern of a vacancy and then a victor reuses the shape of Ezekiel 22:30, and shows what the Old Testament search was awaiting.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's opening chapters show a pair who hid, blamed each other and were sent from the garden, Genesis 3. By Genesis 6 the earth is filled with violence, and the only person who finds favour is Noah, Genesis 6:8 and 11. Ezekiel 22 is the same story at the scale of a city. The word for violence in the flood story, chamas, and the 'bloodshed' of this chapter belong together, and Jerusalem is the Noah-generation's world in miniature. Where Noah's age had one man left to carry the promise, this one has none.

The chapter answers a long-running question: if God gave Israel a land, a Temple and a law, why does it end in ruin? The answer is not that the gifts were inadequate, nor that God abandoned the project. The gifts were met by forgetting, and the covenant's own sanctions, long described in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28, fell. Scattering among the nations, verse 15, is the sentence Moses had named.

It sets up the great waiting of the exile and beyond. After the fall, the prophets keep asking who will stand in the gap. Daniel prays for his people as one of them, Daniel 9:3 to 19. Nehemiah rebuilds the wall, and Ezra weeps over the law's neglect. These are real answers, but partial ones. The people who return are still a people who forget, and the unfinished business of Ezekiel 22:30 remains.

The New Testament says the gap is filled. Jesus is the mediator the search required, 1 Timothy 2:5, and He stands there with His own blood, Hebrews 9:12. He does what no one else could, taking the wrath of verse 31 and removing the dross not by destroying His people but by cleansing them, Titus 2:14. Those He saves are no longer the city of bloodshed but a people for His own possession.

The story closes in a city where the opposite is true. The new Jerusalem has no temple, because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, and nothing impure will ever enter it, Revelation 21:22 to 27. The wall that no one repaired is there as a wall of salvation, Isaiah 60:18, and the gates are never shut. The people who forgot God are replaced by a people who see His face, Revelation 22:4, and the intercessor who stood in the gap is the one on the throne.

quiz.q: What title does God give Jerusalem at the start of this chapter's indictment?

options.text: The city of bloodshed.
options.note: Verse 2 names Jerusalem directly as 'the city of bloodshed,' the central charge of the whole chapter.

options.text: The city of peace and justice.
options.note: This directly contradicts the chapter's sustained indictment of violence and injustice.

options.text: The city of the temple.
options.note: While the temple is Jerusalem's most sacred site, this chapter's title for the city centers on bloodshed, not its sanctuary.

options.text: The city of exiles.
options.note: Exile is the coming judgment described later in the chapter, not the title given to the city at its opening.

quiz.q: Which classes of people specifically mistreat the vulnerable according to verse 7?

options.text: Only foreign invaders mistreat Jerusalem's own vulnerable citizens.
options.note: Verse 7 describes mistreatment happening within Jerusalem itself, by its own people, not by outside invaders.

options.text: Parents are treated with contempt, and the foreign resident, the fatherless, and the widow are all exploited or oppressed.
options.note: Verse 7 lists exactly these groups as mistreated within Jerusalem's own walls.

options.text: Only the wealthy suffer mistreatment in this account.
options.note: The chapter's concern is specifically for the vulnerable, the fatherless, widows, and foreigners, not the wealthy.

options.text: Only religious leaders are named as victims of mistreatment.
options.note: Verse 7 names parents, foreigners, the fatherless, and widows as victims, not religious leaders specifically.

quiz.q: What image does God use in verses 17-22 to describe coming judgment on Israel?

options.text: A vine transplanted to fertile soil.
options.note: That image belongs to earlier chapters; here the image is metal being smelted in a furnace.

options.text: Israel as dross, melted like metal in a smelting furnace within Jerusalem itself.
options.note: Verses 18-22 describe exactly this image of refining, or smelting, judgment.

options.text: A shepherd gathering scattered sheep back to safety.
options.note: That shepherding image belongs to Ezekiel 34, not this smelting-furnace judgment scene.

options.text: A cedar tree growing taller than all others.
options.note: That cedar imagery belongs to Ezekiel 17 and 31, not this chapter's furnace image.

quiz.q: According to verses 25-29, which groups within Jerusalem are named as corrupt?

options.text: Princes, priests, officials, prophets, and the people of the land, all named in turn.
options.note: Verses 25-29 systematically indict each of these groups by name.

options.text: Only the reigning king is named as corrupt in this passage.
options.note: The passage names a full range of classes, not the king alone, who is not specifically singled out here.

options.text: Only foreign officials stationed in Jerusalem.
options.note: The corrupt groups named are Jerusalem's own princes, priests, officials, prophets, and people, not foreign officials.

options.text: Only the priests and prophets, with officials and princes exempted.
options.note: Princes and officials are also explicitly named as corrupt in verses 25 and 27, not exempted.

quiz.q: What does God say He searched for in verse 30, and what did He find?

options.text: A wealthy patron to fund the temple's repair, and he found several willing donors.
options.note: The search described is for a moral and spiritual intercessor, not a financial patron, and none was found.

options.text: A man to repair the wall and stand in the gap on the land's behalf, and He found no one.
options.note: Verse 30 states this search and its stark outcome directly.

options.text: A new king to replace Zedekiah, and He found a suitable candidate.
options.note: The search is for an intercessor to avert judgment, not a replacement king, and no one was found.

options.text: A prophet to warn the city, and He found several faithful prophets.
options.note: The chapter has just described the prophets themselves as corrupt, verse 28; the search in verse 30 ends in finding no one at all.

questions: Jerusalem is charged with forgetting God even while going through the motions of religious life. Where might your own routine or busyness be quietly crowding out actual remembrance of God?

The catalogue of sins in this chapter includes the powerful exploiting the vulnerable, the fatherless, the widow, the foreign resident. Who are the vulnerable people in your own community that you might be overlooking or, worse, benefiting from at their expense?

God pictures His people as dross needing the fire of judgment to expose what is base and worthless. Is there an area of your life you have avoided examining honestly because you fear what the process might expose?
Every class of leadership in Jerusalem, princes, priests, officials, prophets, is found corrupt in this chapter. Where do you place too much confidence in human leadership rather than in God Himself?

God searched for one person to stand in the gap and found no one, until Christ. How does knowing Jesus is your perfect, permanent intercessor change how you pray for the people and situations you feel most helpless about?

translationNotes.note: 'Uncovered the nakedness of their fathers' echoes the specific language of forbidden sexual relations in Leviticus 18, cataloguing violations of the holiness code rather than introducing new categories of sin.

The list of base metals, copper, tin, iron, and lead, mixed with silver, reflects the ancient metallurgical process of refining silver, in which base metals had to be separated out and discarded as worthless dross, sig.

'Stand in the gap' translates language describing an intercessor who blocks a breach in a city's defensive wall, here used metaphorically of someone whose righteousness or intercession might have blocked God's judgment from breaking through against the land.
